title-group.article-title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Colchicine and Anti–Interleukin‐1 Agents in Recurrent Pericarditis: A Pairwise and Network Meta‐Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The management of recurrent pericarditis includes colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents, given the limited efficacy and adverse effects of NSAIDs and corticosteroids. We conducted a pairwise and network meta‐analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents in recurrent pericarditis.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a comprehensive search on various databases to retrieve relevant randomized controlled trials. Pairwise meta‐analyses were performed in R using the exact Mantel–Haenszel method. We also performed a network meta‐analysis with a colchicine group as the comparator.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 6 randomized controlled trials were included in the meta‐analysis. The risk of pericarditis recurrence was significantly decreased by colchicine (risk ratio [RR], 0.46 [95% CI, 0.37–0.58]) and anti–interleukin‐1 agents (RR, 0.12 [95% CI, 0.03–0.54]) compared with placebo or standard therapy. Colchicine significantly decreased the risk of treatment failure (RR, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.31–0.57]) and pericarditis‐related rehospitalization (RR, 0.26 [95% CI, 0.10–0.70]) but did not have a significant impact on the risk of adverse events (RR, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.31–3.62]). Anti–interleukin‐1 agents were associated with a significantly increased risk of adverse events (RR, 1.88 [95% CI, 1.60–2.21]). The network meta‐analysis showed that anti–interleukin‐1 agents were associated with a greater reduction in pericarditis recurrence than colchicine (RR, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.11–0.67]), with no significant difference with respect to adverse events (RR, 1.77 [95% CI, 0.88–3.57]).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Both colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents are effective in reducing the risk of recurrent pericarditis. Anti–interleukin‐1 agents are associated with more frequent nonserious adverse events, but evidence on serious adverse events remains inconclusive.
Keywords: colchicine, network meta‐analysis, RCTs, recurrence, recurrent pericarditis

list-item.p: This network meta‐analysis demonstrates that anti–interleukin‐1 agents have superior efficacy in the management of recurrent pericarditis compared with colchicine.

Both colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents significantly reduce pericarditis recurrence, but anti–interleukin‐1 therapies may be considered earlier in the management algorithm, especially in colchicine‐resistant cases.

While anti–interleukin‐1 agents are associated with a higher risk of mild to moderate adverse events, current evidence remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions regarding serious adverse event risk.

body.p: Recurrent pericarditis is the appearance of clinical manifestations of pericardial inflammation after a symptom‐free period of 4 to 6 weeks following an episode of acute pericarditis. 1 The first‐line medications used for acute pericarditis, such as NSAIDs and corticosteroids, do not have a substantial benefit in recurrent cases. 1 Colchicine, a microtubule inhibitor and nonspecific inflammasome inhibitor, has been found effective in managing recurrent pericarditis according to several systematic reviews. 2 , 3 , 4

Recent research indicates that excessive activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome contributes to the generation of proinflammatory molecules of the interleukin‐1 family and underlies the pathogenesis of idiopathic recurrent pericarditis. 5 , 6 Furthermore, interleukin‐1 stimulates the production of various inflammatory molecules, such as cyclo‐oxygenase and prostaglandins, which significantly contribute to systemic inflammation associated with recurrent pericarditis. 6 , 7

Hence, anti–interleukin‐1 agents including rilonacept and anakinra have been investigated for the management of recurrent pericarditis. 8 , 9 More recently, a randomized controlled trial (RCT) assessing the role of goflikicept, a novel heterodimeric anti–interleukin‐1 agent, was also published. 10 The comparative efficacy of these treatments has not been comprehensively assessed previously. We aimed to conduct a pairwise and network meta‐analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents for recurrent pericarditis.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This meta‐analysis was conducted following the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses statement. 11 We registered the study protocol with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews of Interventions with the identification number CRD42024604330. This study did not require any ethical approval. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

sec.title: Information Sources and Search Process
sec.p: We performed a systematic search of MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to April 2024 to retrieve RCTs investigating colchicine or anti–interleukin‐1 agents in patients with recurrent pericarditis. We also screened the reference lists of relevant RCTs and systematic reviews to identify further eligible articles.

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria
sec.p: The inclusion criteria were (1) study design: randomized controlled trials (RCTs) only; (2) patient population: patients with recurrent pericarditis; (3) intervention: colchicine with/without NSAIDs or anti–interleukin‐1 agents; (4) control: placebo or standard treatment; and (5) outcome: reporting at least 1 outcome of interest. We excluded studies that (1) included patients with acute pericarditis; (2) were not RCTs (ie, observational studies: case series, case–control studies, and cohort studies); and (3) were done in animal populations.

sec.title: Study Screening and Data Extraction
sec.p: The literature obtained from our searches was imported into Zotero 6.0.36 (Corporation for Digital Scholarship, Vienna, VA) where duplicates were removed. Two authors independently carried out the title/abstract and full‐text screening of the studies in consecutive phases. Any disagreements were resolved via discussion.

A structured spreadsheet was used to extract the relevant study characteristics and outcomes. Our primary outcome was the recurrence of pericarditis, and secondary outcomes included treatment failure, pericarditis‐related rehospitalization, adverse events, and serious adverse events (SAEs). The return of symptoms and signs of pericarditis following a 4‐ to 6‐week asymptomatic period after an episode of acute pericarditis constitutes a recurrence. 12 Treatment failure is defined as the persistence of symptoms of pericarditis after 72 hours of treatment. We synthesized adverse events and SAEs using the criteria defined by the individual RCTs.

sec.title: Risk‐of‐Bias Assessment
sec.p: The revised Cochrane “Risk of Bias” tool for randomized trials (RoB 2.0) was used to assess the risk of bias in the included trials. 13

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All pairwise and network meta‐analyses were performed in R version 4.3.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). For binary outcomes, we used the exact Mantel–Haenszel method, which provides accurate estimates without reliance on large‐sample approximations and is particularly suited for studies with small or zero event counts. The effect measure was the risk ratio (RR) with 95% CIs. Both fixed‐effect and random‐effect models were calculated, but random‐effect estimates are reported as the primary results, given their broader generalizability and consistency with anticipated clinical heterogeneity. Fixed‐effect results are provided in forest plots for reference. 14 The Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman adjustment was applied to the 95% CIs. For each analysis, we used the χ2 test and I 2 statistics to assess heterogeneity. Additionally, we performed a network meta‐analysis under a frequentist model with colchicine group as the comparator. The geometry of the treatment network was visualized using network plots, and relative treatment effects were presented in forest plots. To assess the robustness of the network meta‐analysis findings, we also conducted a Bayesian sensitivity analysis using a binomial likelihood and log link function. All the analyses were performed in Meta Insight (Complex Reviews Support Unit) version 6.3. We aimed to assess publication bias using funnel plot and Egger's regression test if the number of studies in a meta‐analysis was >10.

sec.title: Study Selection and Characteristics
sec.p: We included a total of 6 RCTs in our review. 10 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses flowchart was constructed to depict the study selection process (Figure 1). Three RCTs investigated colchicine (doses between 0.5 and 1.2 mg/d), and 3 investigated anti–interleukin‐1 agents. The detailed study characteristics of the included RCTs are presented in Table 1. The eligibility criteria of individual RCTs are presented in Table S1.

sec.title: Risk‐of‐Bias Assessment
sec.p: Four of the 6 RCTs included in this review were assessed to have a low risk of bias, while 2 had some concerns (Figure 2). These concerns primarily stemmed from problems with the randomization process and selective reporting of results. Specifically, the AIRTRIP (Anakinra‐Treatment of Recurrent Idiopathic Pericarditis) and CORE (Colchicine for Recurrent Pericarditis) trials did not clarify whether allocation concealment was maintained until the patients were randomized into their respective groups. Additionally, the CORE trial lacked a pre‐published trial protocol to indicate predefined outcomes and a statistical analysis plan.

sec.title: Primary Outcome
sec.p: Our meta‐analysis found that colchicine decreased the risk of pericarditis recurrence compared with placebo/standard therapy (RR, 0.46 [95% CI, 0.37–0.58]; Figure 3). Similarly, anti–interleukin‐1 agents were also associated with a significantly decreased risk of pericarditis recurrence (RR, 0.12 [95% CI, 0.03–0.54]; Figure 3). Heterogeneity in both analyses was minimal (I 2=0%).

sec.title: Secondary Outcomes
sec.p: The risk of treatment failure was significantly decreased in the colchicine group (RR, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.31–0.57]; Figure S1) with minimal heterogeneity (I 2=0%). Colchicine did not significantly impact the risk of adverse events (RR, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.31–3.62]; I 2=0%; Figure 4). Anti–interleukin‐1 agents were associated with a significantly increased risk of adverse events (RR, 1.88 [95% CI, 1.60–2.21]; Figure 4). The most common adverse events were injection site reactions, upper respiratory tract infections, and infections. Only 1 of 11 patients had an infection with anakinra while 6 of 10 and 12 of 30 patients had an infection/infestation with goflikicept and rilonacept, respectively. For SAEs, only 6 events were reported across studies, precluding reliable meta‐analysis. No SAEs were reported among patients receiving colchicine. Descriptive data suggest low event rates in both treatment and control arms (1/30 versus 1/30 in RHAPSODY [Phase 3 Trial of Interleukin‐1 Trap Rilonacept in Recurrent Pericarditis] and 2/10 versus 2/10 in Myachikova et al10), but the limited number of events prevents firm conclusions about differences in SAE risk. Only 2 studies have assessed the risk of pericarditis‐related rehospitalization. Colchicine was associated with a decreased risk of pericarditis‐related rehospitalization (RR, 0.26 [95% CI, 0.10–0.70]; Figure S2).

sec.title: Results of the Network Meta‐Analysis
sec.p: The network meta‐analysis showed that the anti–interleukin‐1 agents were associated with a greater reduction in pericarditis recurrence than colchicine (RR, 0.27 [95% CI, 0.11–0.67]; Figure 5, Figure S3). These results were corroborated by Bayesian analysis, which demonstrated consistent effect estimates (Figure S4). All anti–interleukin‐1 agents significantly decreased the risk of pericarditis recurrence, with comparable efficacies among the different agents (Figure S5). No significantly increased risk of adverse events was seen with anti–interleukin‐1 agents when compared with colchicine (RR, 1.77 [95% CI, 0.88–3.57]; Figure 6, Figure S6). The Bayesian analysis demonstrated consistent results (Figure S7).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first network meta‐analysis to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of different treatment options for recurrent pericarditis. Our findings indicate that colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents reduce the risk of pericarditis recurrence compared with placebo/standard therapy. These results are consistent with prior meta‐analyses assessing various drug treatments against placebo or standard therapy. 8 , 9 , 20 Notably, the anti–interleukin‐1 agents were found to be more efficacious than colchicine.

A meta‐analysis by Melendo‐Viu et al found a significant reduction in the recurrence of pericarditis with colchicine and anakinra. 20 However, their analysis also included studies in patients with acute pericarditis. By contrast, our analysis exclusively included trials involving patients with recurrent pericarditis, thereby enhancing the validity of our findings. Furthermore, they did not include the 2 most recent trials by Klein et al 18 and Myachikova et al 10 that investigated the effects of rilonacept and goflikicept in recurrent pericarditis. The efficacy of colchicine in acute and recurrent pericarditis has also been validated in other systematic reviews. 2 , 3 , 4 Colchicine inhibits tubulin polymerization, thus disrupting phagocytosis and mitigating the inflammatory pathways associated with recurrent pericarditis. 21

Our network meta‐analysis revealed that anti–interleukin‐1 agents exhibited superior efficacy over colchicine in the treatment of recurrent pericarditis. The European Society of Cardiology Guidelines recommend corticosteroids as a second‐line and interleukin‐1 inhibitors as a third‐line option for pericarditis. 1 While corticosteroids quickly control symptoms, they can promote chronic conditions, increase the likelihood of recurrences, and cause various side effects. Corticosteroids at low to moderate doses should be avoided if infections cannot be ruled out. Given the chronic nature of recurrent pericarditis, the long‐term use of corticosteroids is not feasible owing to serious adverse effects. Recurrences during the taper of corticosteroids further complicate the management. 22 Our network meta‐analysis indicates that anti–interleukin‐1 agents are not only more effective than colchicine but also possess a favorable safety profile, prompting reconsideration of their role. However, shorter treatment times with colchicine may reduce long‐term risks and associated side effects, which may be seen as a practical advantage over the prolonged use of anti–interleukin‐1 agents. Additionally, they can be quite costly, especially as a long‐term therapy, and might involve more complex treatment regimens and monitoring. 23 , 24 Despite promising findings, there is a lack of sufficient data, especially concerning accessibility and discontinuation, to claim the superiority of anti–interleukin‐1 agents over colchicine, which has a long history of use and offers greater confidence in its therapeutic benefits. Hence, our results propose that anti–interleukin‐1 agents could be more appropriate as a second‐line treatment option, especially for cases refractory to colchicine and NSAIDs. 1 Our meta‐analysis supports the recent positional statement by Klein et al, which recommends anti–interleukin‐1 agents (anakinra, rilonacept, goflikicept) as alternatives to corticosteroids highlighting recent advances beyond previous guidelines by the American Society of Echocardiography and the European Society of Cardiology. 25 Recent meta‐analyses comparing anakinra or rilonacept with placebo/standard therapy have reported a significant reduction in pericarditis recurrence with these drugs. 8 , 9 Affas et al 9 included a retrospective cohort study along with 3 trials in their analysis; results from 2 uncontrolled studies were also incorporated into their meta‐analysis.

We also found a significantly increased risk of adverse events with anti–interleukin‐1 agents in our meta‐analysis. This finding aligns with the prior systematic review by Imazio et al 8 , which found a significantly greater risk of adverse events associated with the use of rilonacept and anakinra. Moreover, they did not find an increased risk of SAEs. It is, however, noteworthy that goflikicept was associated with a higher rate of adverse events as compared with those reported previously. This could possibly be related to the fact that the study started at the beginning of the COVID‐19 pandemic and that the adverse effects were driven by an underlying infection. Moreover, the results of our network meta‐analysis found no significantly increased risk of adverse events with anti–interleukin‐1 agents when compared with colchicine.

Additionally, our network meta‐analysis revealed that the efficacy of the different anti–interleukin‐1 agents was comparable with each other. However, the comparative efficacy of these agents should be interpreted with caution, as only 1 RCT was done for each anti–interleukin‐1 agent, and the availability of these agents varies across European countries and North America. 10

This is the first network meta‐analysis to compare colchicine with anti–interleukin‐1 agents for the treatment of recurrent pericarditis. We pooled data from recent trials and provided comprehensive evidence by examining all the available literature. Previous meta‐analyses included observational studies in addition to RCTs, whereas our analysis only pooled data from RCTs, which increased the quality of the evidence provided by our results. Moreover, minimal heterogeneity was observed in all analyses, and most of the studies exhibited a low risk of bias. This is also the first analysis to consider the novel anti–interleukin‐1 agent, goflikicept.

Despite the promising findings of this analysis, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the heterogeneity of study designs presents a significant challenge. The patient populations in colchicine trials are fundamentally different from those in interleukin‐1 inhibitor trials; interleukin‐1 inhibitor trials typically enroll patients who have failed colchicine therapy and, in many cases, have also struggled to taper off prednisone, indicating a population that is generally sicker than that in colchicine trials. Furthermore, anti‐interleukin‐1 treatments often involve longer durations than colchicine, with differing follow‐up periods, which may affect comparative outcomes. Additionally, there were some minor differences in diagnostic criteria of recurrences that introduced variability, potentially obscuring the true effect of the interventions being studied. Furthermore, the duration of follow‐up varied between studies, with some trials assessing outcomes over short periods (eg, 6 months), while others had longer follow‐up periods (eg, 20 months). This variability in follow‐up duration may influence the assessment of long‐term recurrence and outcomes, adding an additional layer of complexity to interpreting the results. Concomitant therapies also vary between trials, further complicating direct comparisons. Another limitation is the potential variation in efficacy across different anti‐interleukin‐1 agents, as it remains unclear if they exert equivalent effects in treating pericarditis. In addition, the anti–interleukin‐1 trials used a randomized withdrawal study design which may impact the event rate among patients assigned to placebo. The small number of events, especially within the anti‐interleukin‐1 trials, reduces the statistical power of the analysis, limiting the strength of conclusions that can be drawn. Additionally, data pooling for other efficacy outcomes, such as symptomatic improvement and changes in inflammatory markers, was challenging, leading to an incomplete assessment of these parameters. The network meta‐analysis was structurally limited by the absence of head‐to‐head trials between active treatments, and all comparisons were made indirectly through a shared placebo group. This design restricts the ability to formally assess network coherence, consistency, and transitivity assumptions. In view of the foregoing, the results of our network meta‐analysis must be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis generating rather than definitive evidence. Insufficient data and reporting prevented us from conducting subgroup analyses and assessing other outcomes, such as time to pericarditis recurrence. The potential impact of continuing other medications or tapering corticosteroids could not be accounted for in this analysis. Finally, the potential for publication bias should be considered, as studies with positive findings are more likely to be published, potentially skewing the results of this analysis. To address these limitations, future large‐scale, well‐designed randomized controlled trials that directly compare treatment options are necessary to establish more robust evidence. Moreover, pharmacoeconomic considerations should be considered when suggesting a long‐term therapy, and additional research should be developed on combination therapies that could minimize side effects, improve tolerability, efficacy and reduce duration of therapies and management costs.

Several clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate the role of novel medications in recurrent pericarditis, particularly in colchicine‐resistant cases. The CREATE (Therapeutic Approach in Colchicine‐Resistant Recurrent Pericarditis in Children; ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT05805930) trial is an open‐label study comparing anakinra with corticosteroids in colchicine‐resistant recurrent pericarditis. 26 MAVERIC (Impact of CardiolRxTM Over 6 Months Following IL‐1 Blocker Cessation in Pericarditis Patients), a double‐blind RCT, is evaluating the role of CardiolRx in patients with recurrent pericarditis following cessation of anti–interleukin‐1 agents. 27 A few trials are assessing the role of novel medications, namely VTX2735 and KPL‐387 in the management of recurrent pericarditis. 28 , 29 However, no ongoing trials have directly compared colchicine with anti–interleukin‐1 agents, highlighting a gap in the current literature.

In conclusion, colchicine and anti–interleukin‐1 agents are effective in reducing the risk of pericarditis recurrence with the anti–interleukin‐1 agents demonstrating greater efficacy, albeit at a higher cost. These findings advocate for more flexibility in treatment strategies, emphasizing that newer agents with comparable or superior efficacy might need to be integrated earlier in the treatment algorithm, pending further research. This analysis could influence updates to future pericardial disease guidelines, supporting earlier use of anti–interleukin‐1 agents in recurrent pericarditis and prompting further high‐quality research to optimize treatment strategies. Further large‐scale RCTs that directly compare various treatment options are needed to confirm or refute our findings.
